newsitem.title: JAPAN: New Japan power plan draws fire from utilities.
newsitem.headline: New Japan power plan draws fire from utilities.

text.p: A new report aimed at stirring up fresh competition within Japan's relatively cloistered electric utility network has come under fire from some domestic power companies, industry sources said on Tuesday.
The study, issued by Japan's Fair Trade Commission (FTC), promotes the division of electric power utilities into producers and distributors in order to make room for new players in the marketplace.

Viewed by some foreign analysts as a positive step in the direction of the free-wheeling power markets taking shape in the United Kingdom, Australia and California, the report has also been criticised from within Japan as encouraging quick profit at the expense of a more prudent energy policy.

"This report was compiled solely from the viewpoint of how to promote competition, setting aside issues such as energy security and the environment," a Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) official said.
"We believe energy policies ought to be discussed from various perspectives," he said.
The FTC report is the latest example of steady government efforts to whip electricity prices into line with overseas levels since reforms were first launched last year.
Industry estimates show the average family in Japan pays about 20 percent more for its electricity than a German family and 30 percent more than a family in the United States.

Currently, each of Japan's 10 private electric power firms, which enjoy regional monopolies in exchange for dependable supplies, is vertically integrated, with generation and distribution sectors operating in tandem.
A division of power firms into generators and distributors, as suggested in the FTC report, was carried out in the U.K. in 1990.
Electricity prices in the U.K. have declined by about 11 percent since the division, a MITI report said.
But some analysts say the U.K.'s bountiful domestic resources and static power demand make a comparison with Japan difficult.
"Constant growth in electricity demand like in Japan requires vertically integrated power firms," a spokesman for the Federation of Electric Power Companies said.

"Japan needs to build new power plants every year to keep up with increasing electricity demand, and firms with both production and distribution sectors would best be able to carry out huge investments of that sort," he said.
"Japan is also more sensitive to energy supply security," another analyst said.

Masanori Maruo, a senior analyst for Daiwa Institute of Research, also suggests that the introduction of smaller, cost-cutting, independent power producers, or IPPs, will increase Japan's dependence on imported oil for power production. "Too much emphasis on efficiency will drive power generators to cheaper thermal power production, which runs counter to Japan's fundamental energy policies," he said.
Japan, which imports more than 99 percent of its crude oil requirements, has been trying to strike the best balance in power generation between nuclear, hydro and thermal production.
Thermal power plants running on crude or heavy fuel oil accounted for 63 percent of Japan's total power output in 1975.
But Japan has squeezed the percentage to about 17 percent since then, while raising the ratio of electricity from nuclear power plants to 34 percent from 6 percent.
